transcript.text: I made the mistake of telling a friend
about this this idea. Now he's acting
like it's our idea and assuming he's a
co-founder. I want to take this back and
build it solo. How do I walk this back
without it getting ugly?
>> This is awesome.
Um, welcome to entrepreneurship. Welcome
to your first hard conversation that you
get to have. I actually had this exact
same situation happen to me. So when I
first started Gym Launch, one of the
launches was at a gym owner who had a
gym marketing agency. And after I did
it, he said, "Hey, let's go out to
dinner. Let's talk." He brought his his
uh his partner in and he was like, "Hey,
so, you know, let's partner and do this.
I already have all these gyms that are
my customers. You have this thing, you
know, let's partner on it." And I
remember this being one of the hardest
moments of my life. Like I became a man
in business when I was able to look at a
older guy who was more experienced and
say,
"I'm going to do this on my own." And he
said, "Well, I mean, if you're going to
do this on your own," he's like, "I'm
going to do this, too." Uh and I already
have all the customers.
And I said then I guess we're just going
to compete then. You just have to decide
what's more important to you, which is
am I going to split all of my earnings
for the rest of my life on this business
because I don't want to have one hard
conversation.
